goal: `mc test <repo> --full` runs what that repository calls its whole suite, mc runs it on its own on an interval, and the answer says which tests are red on `main` **and since when**. Report only: nothing here refuses a merge, blocks a round, or changes what `mc test <repo> <pr>` decides. Ruled by Martin, 2026-09-02.

It does none of that today, and the first half is a false green. `repo-gate.js`'s `suiteCommand` defines a repository's whole suite as its `npm test`, verbatim — a deliberate choice, so that mc keeps no second definition of a repository's suite. For memoro that definition is wrong: `npm test` is `node scripts/testing/ci.mjs`, the affected-selection. With `--full` there is no pull request, so the round checks out `origin/main` detached and the selector diffs `origin/main` against itself. Measured 2026-09-02 with `node scripts/testing/ci.mjs --list --base-ref HEAD` in the memoro worktree: `changed paths: 0`, `selected test files: 6`. **`mc test memoro --full` runs 6 files of 2,018 and reports it as the whole suite.** That is precisely the failure `repo-gate-table.js`'s own header was written against — a run that "runs a *subset* and reports a summary anyway".

The second half does not exist at all. Nothing in memoro is scheduled: every workflow under `.github/workflows/` is `workflow_dispatch:` except `legal-gate.yml`, and GitHub Actions is billing-blocked for this account since 2026-08-04. The whole suite runs only when a person types `npm run test:full`. That is the direct cause of #10529 — four days of merges left 31 surface-runtime tests red on memoro's `main` while every pull request's affected-selection passed, because nothing ever looked at the whole. Measured 2026-09-02, memoro's full suite is 2,018 files, 17,928 tests, **337 s** wall clock, and six tests standing red on `main`. A reading that costs five and a half minutes once a day is not the expensive thing here; not having it is.
contract: Report only. Nothing in this project refuses a merge, delays a round, or changes any verdict `mc test` or `mc merge` produces. A blocking policy — "main has been red for N days, land nothing" — is a separate question and is deliberately not taken here. Ruled by Martin, 2026-09-02.

`--full` never guesses what a repository's whole suite is. It runs a command that was declared, or it stops with a reason — the same rule `repo-gate-table.js` already holds for preparation, and for the same stated reason: a guess that works nine times and quietly reports a green from an incomplete suite on the tenth is worse than a stop, because the stop is visible and the green is not.
The scheduled run writes only under mc's home. It never commits, never pushes, never writes inside a repository, and never takes a branch. It is a meter, like the watcher beside it.

One gate round at a time on this machine still holds. A scheduled full run takes `gate-lock.js` like any other round, and when the lock is held it **skips that tick and records the skip** — it never queues behind a merge round, and never makes one wait 337 s.
No test is added, deleted, weakened or reclassified in any repository by this project. What is red is reported as red.
out_of_scope: What memoro selects for an ordinary diff, and how long memoro's gate takes. That is `test-architecture/test-value-cleanup` and `test-architecture/mc-test` in the memoro repository. This project is the net, not the gate.

Fixing the six tests red on memoro's `main`. The net's whole job is to say that they are red and since when; repairing them is the owning project's work, and a net that waits for a green tree is a net that never ships.
Any blocking or refusing behaviour derived from the nightly answer, including a red-days threshold on `mc merge`. Explicitly deferred by the ruling above.
Hosted CI of any kind. Actions is billing-blocked and every memoro workflow is `workflow_dispatch:`; nothing here dispatches one, schedules one, or depends on one running.

`.mc/test.json` in the memoro repository. mc's shipped table can carry memoro's declaration today and the layering already exists (#502), so this project does not need a memoro pull request to be finished. Moving memoro's entry into memoro's own file is memoro's to do when it wants it.

success_criteria.criterion: `mc test memoro --full` runs memoro's whole suite.
success_criteria.check: Run it. The report names 2,018 test files and a duration in the region of 337 s, against the 6 files it selects today. Cross-check the file count against `npm run test:full` in the memoro worktree.

success_criteria.criterion: A declaration that names a selector but no suite cannot produce a whole-suite answer.
success_criteria.check: A unit test over `declarationFor` and the `--full` path: a declaration with `select` and no `suite` stops with a reason naming both fields. Verified for real by removing memoro's `suite` and seeing `mc test memoro --full` stop rather than run six files.

success_criteria.criterion: The full run happens without anybody asking for it, and never delays a merge round.
success_criteria.check: Two scheduled runs observed in the log across one interval boundary. Then start a merge round, and confirm from the log that the tick that overlapped it recorded a skip with the holding round's pid rather than waiting.

success_criteria.criterion: A red test on main is named with the date it first went red.
success_criteria.check: After two runs that both see `tests/architecture/data-bus.test.js` red, `mc` names it with the timestamp of the first run that saw it, not the latest. Confirmed a second way by hand-editing the stored history to a third, older run and seeing the reported date move back.

success_criteria.criterion: A test that stops being red stops being reported.
success_criteria.check: Take a run's stored result, remove one failing name from it, run again, and confirm the name is gone from the page rather than lingering with an old date.

documents.label: The verb this extends, and the round it must not disturb

steps.title: `--full` runs what the repository calls its whole suite, or it stops
steps.done_when: `mc test memoro --full` reports about 2,018 test files instead of 6; a declaration that carries `select` and no `suite` makes `--full` stop with a reason naming both fields; `mc test memoro-cli --full` behaves exactly as it does today; and the suite command, like `select` and `prepare`, is layered shipped < the repository's `.mc/test.json` < `~/mc/repo-gates.json`.
instruction: Read `repo-gate-table.js`'s header before touching it. Its whole argument is that what a repository needs is written down or the round stops, never guessed, and that a partial declaration which lets a round proceed is "the guess wearing a uniform". This step adds one more thing to write down and applies that same rule to it. Nothing about the layering, the `UNKNOWN` third answer, or the rule that a `_why` may never carry a provenance that does not exist changes here.

The bug, so you do not have to rediscover it: `repo-gate.js:333` sets `selects` false when `--full` is given, line 334 falls to `suiteCommand({ repoPath })`, and `suiteCommand` at line 858 returns the repository's `npm test`. For memoro that is `node scripts/testing/ci.mjs` — the affected-selection — and with no pull request the round measures `origin/main` against `origin/main`, so the diff is empty. Measured 2026-09-02: 6 files. The comment above `suiteCommand` is not wrong about *why* mc should not invent a suite command; it is wrong to assume `npm test` is always the whole one.

Add `suite` and `suite_why` to the declaration, beside `select` and `select_why`, read through `declarationFor` with the same three layers and the same unknown-key discipline. `suite` is the command to run for `--full`. Then the narrow rule that makes the guess impossible: **a declaration that carries `select` and does not carry `suite` may not answer a `--full` — it stops, and the reason names both fields.** A repository that declares a selector has already said, by declaring one, that `npm test` is not the whole thing. A repository with no `select` keeps today's behaviour exactly: `npm test`, verbatim, no declaration needed.

Fill both shipped entries, and make the `_why` carry a real measurement rather than a claim. memoro: `suite: 'npm run test:full'`, and the evidence is this project's own measurement of 2026-09-02 — 2,018 files, 17,928 tests, 337.42 s wall, six tests red on `main`, on an Apple M1 with 8 GB, machine not idle. memoro-cli: `suite: 'npm test'`, and the evidence is that its `test` script is `node --test --import ./tests/_isolate-home.mjs 'tests/**/*.test.js'`, a glob over the whole tree, which is why it needs a declaration that says so rather than an exemption from the rule.

Two things in the report have to follow. `report.command` already carries what was run, so a reader can see it; make sure the whole-suite phrasing at `repo-gate.js:624-630` still tells the truth — there are two different "whole suite" sentences there, one for `--full` asked for and one for a selector that gave up and fell back, and they must not converge now that `--full` means something different. And the round's own record (`full_suite` at line 427) should say which command produced it, not just that it was full.

Verify by running it, not by reading it: `mc test memoro --full` before the change reports 6 files, after it reports about 2,018 and takes minutes. Then remove memoro's `suite` from the shipped table in a throwaway edit and confirm the round stops rather than falling back to six files — that negative is the one that matters, because it is the shape the bug had.
comments: **`--full` is six files, and the code says why in three lines**

`repo-gate.js:333` — `const selects = Boolean(declared.declaration.select) && !wholeSuite;` — so `--full` turns the selector *off* and falls to `suiteCommand({ repoPath })` at line 334. `suiteCommand` (line 858) reads `package.json` and returns `npm test`, with a comment explaining the choice: mc must not keep its own idea of a repository's suite. The reasoning is right; the assumption underneath it — that a repository's `npm test` runs everything — is not true of memoro.

With no pull request the round checks out the default branch detached (`repo-gate.js:340`), so `npm test` runs `ci.mjs` against `origin/main` on `origin/main`. Measured in the memoro worktree 2026-09-02: `node scripts/testing/ci.mjs --list --base-ref HEAD` → `changed paths: 0`, `selected test files: 6`, `commands: (none)`. The six are the mandatory core.

The narrow rule that catches this without mc learning anything about any named repository: **a declaration that carries `select` and no `suite` may not answer a `--full`.** A repository that declares a selector has, by declaring it, said that `npm test` is not the whole thing. Checked against both repositories mc knows: memoro's `npm test` is `node scripts/testing/ci.mjs` (a selector — must declare `suite`), memoro-cli's is `node --test --import ./tests/_isolate-home.mjs 'tests/**/*.test.js'` (a glob over everything — declares `suite: 'npm test'` and is telling the truth).
**Nothing in memoro is scheduled, and that is #10529's cause**

Every workflow under memoro's `.github/workflows/` is `on: workflow_dispatch:` except `legal-gate.yml` (`on: pull_request`, paths `public/lang/**`). Checked file by file 2026-09-02. GitHub Actions is billing-blocked for this account since 2026-08-04, so this is not an accident to be corrected by turning a trigger back on — it is the standing condition this project has to work inside.

So the whole suite runs when a person types `npm run test:full` and at no other time. #10529 is what that produces: four days of merges, 31 surface-runtime tests red on `main`, every pull request green. memoro's answer to that was to make its gate run the whole `msr-contract` profile for any diff under `public/js/msr/` — 325 files on every MSR change, about 213 s of a 234 s round, and 34 % of memoro's last 150 landings touch that directory. **The blanket is a substitute for this net**, paid roughly thirteen times a day instead of once.

Measured 2026-09-02 on this machine (Apple M1, 8 cores, 8 GB): memoro's `npm run test:full` is 2,018 files, 17,928 tests, 337.42 s wall, ~808 s summed CPU across 7 lanes, six tests red on `main`. One run a day is a twentieth of what the blanket costs a day.
**Where the pieces already are**

`gate-lock.js` is the one-round-at-a-time guard: a file and a pid under mc's home, `taken` and the pid alive → refused with the round's identity; taken and the pid gone → take it; no expiry, because no clock can tell a slow round from a dead one. It is exactly the door a scheduled run must knock on, and its own header says it never blocks anything but a gate round.

`repo-watch.js` / `repo-watch-loop.js` / `repo-snapshot.js` are the existing meter: a detached node process with a pid file and a log, a round every `DEFAULT_INTERVAL_MS` (60 s), writing atomically under `~/mc/repo-status/` and never inside a repository. Its round is seconds; a full suite is 337 s. The cadences cannot share a loop — but the shape (detached, pid file, atomic snapshot, optional, and the view says which way it answered) is the shape to copy, and `writeJsonAtomic` is already the one door that makes a file appear whole.

**Done, and measured on both sides.** `--full` now runs the `suite` the declaration names. At memoro's `58db0f5` the same tree gives 6 files from `npm test` (`node scripts/testing/ci.mjs --list`: `changed paths: 0, selected test files: 6`) and 2,021 from `npm run test:full` (`run.mjs --profile full --list`: standard 1,770, sqlite 243, heavy 8). The round itself: 17,982 tests, 6 fail, 3 process summaries, 288.3 s of suite inside 302.3 s wall, `full_suite: {command: "npm run test:full", source: "declared"}`. memoro-cli's round is unchanged — the same commit `7e0f84d`, the same 2,440 tests, 40 failures and 47 red names as the identical round driven by unmodified `origin/main` mc, and the two `--json` reports differ only in timings, holder, and the two new fields.

**The operator table on this machine shadows the shipped entry, and that is the third instance of D-0135.** `~/.memoro/mc/repo-gates.json` carries a whole-entry override for memoro, so the shipped `suite` could not reach it: with the source change alone, `mc test memoro --full` stopped with `DECLARATION SHADOWED — the override for memoro omits suite`. I declared `suite`/`suite_why` in that file too (a machine-local file, outside both repositories, backed up first to `/tmp/repo-gates.json.bak-20260903T074723`) and the round then ran. The shadow warning did its job — this is the mechanism working, not failing — but it means every field this table gains has to be restated in the operator's file by hand, for memoro, for as long as that override exists. The plan's out-of-scope note says the shipped table can carry memoro's declaration today; on this machine it cannot, and a later step that assumes it can will stop the same way.

**The negative was verified for real, not only in a unit test.** With memoro's `suite` renamed away in a throwaway edit, `mc test memoro --full` stopped at `suite` naming both fields and both places to write them, and ran nothing — no worktree, no `npm ci`, no six files. That is the shape the bug had, and it is now a stop.

**The red set on memoro's main has already moved from the one in this plan.** At `58db0f5` on 2026-09-03 it is eight names over five files: `data-bus event names come from a single source file`; three under `S3.1 canonical mutation inventory`; `Signals runtime, routes, commands, and surfaces stay retired`; two under `mc context`; and `append enforces first/next/gap/parent/anchor and exact duplicate semantics`. `tests/ui/theme-contract.test.js` is no longer red, and the `append` one is new since 2026-09-02. Step 3's "since when" has nothing stored to compare against yet, and this is the drift it exists to make visible — the list in the plan is a day old and already wrong in two places.

**Two smaller decisions inside the step.** The report now names the npm script behind an npm command (`npm test  (node --test …)`, `npm run test:full  (node scripts/testing/run.mjs --profile full)`), because `npm run test:full` and `npm test` read identically and differ by 2,015 files — this also keeps memoro-cli's `command` line byte-identical to what it printed before. And `full_suite` on the report is a *different field* from `selection.full_suite`: the first is which command a whole-suite round ran, the second is the selector's admission that it could not narrow a change. They are never both set, because the first exists only when no selection ran.

**Worth knowing for step 2.** memoro's `npm run test:full` runs three sequential `node --test` processes (standard/sqlite/heavy) and prints one TAP summary each; `tapTotals` sums them, which it was already built to do. `prepare` for memoro is `npm ci` and cost 8.9 s here, not the minutes the tree size suggests. So a scheduled round is about 300 s of gate lock for memoro and about 70 s for memoro-cli — the numbers the tick's skip policy has to be sized against.

steps.title: The run nobody asks for, that never gets in a round's way
steps.done_when: A full run happens on an interval with no person involved, recorded in a log with its start, its duration, the commit of `main` it measured, and its result; a tick that finds `gate-lock.js` held records a skip naming the holding round and does not wait; and stopping the scheduler stops it, with no orphan process and no stale pid file.
instruction: This is a second meter, not a second watcher. `repo-watch.js` rounds in seconds every 60 s; a full round is 337 s for one repository. They cannot share a loop, and squeezing a 337 s round into a 60 s cadence is how a machine ends up running two of them at once. Copy the *shape* rather than the loop: a detached node process, a pid file checked against the process table and against the runner's command line (pids are reused — `repo-watch.js:watcherState` already does exactly this check and it is the part that is easy to get wrong), a log capped like `LOG_LIMIT_BYTES`, `writeJsonAtomic` for everything it writes, and everything under mc's home.

Take `gate-lock.js` for the round, and read its header first — it is the one door the big suites go through, and its argument is that there is no honest expiry because a round is supposed to take minutes. So the scheduled run does not wait, does not retry in a tight loop, and does not force. It attempts the lock; if the lock is held by a live pid, the tick is over and the skip is written down with that pid and the time. A skipped tick is a fact about the day, not an error — a machine that merged all evening should show a night of skips and one run, and that should read as normal rather than as a failure.

The cadence is Martin's day, not a cron expression pulled from habit. Default it to once a day and make the interval configurable in the same place mc's other intervals live; do not invent a new configuration surface for it. Whether it fires at a wall-clock hour or simply every N hours since the last completed run is yours to choose — but choose the one that behaves sanely when the laptop was asleep at the appointed hour, and say in the code comment which you chose and why, because the other one is what a reader will assume.

It runs `mc test <repo> --full` for each repository mc knows, through the same code path a person's `--full` goes through. Not a copy of it, and not `npm run test:full` directly: the whole value is that the scheduled reading and the asked-for reading cannot disagree, which is the same argument `repo-watch-loop.js` makes about its own round using the ordinary aggregator.

Do not build a queue, a retry policy, a backoff, or a notion of a run that is "overdue". A missed night is a missed night; the next tick runs. The previous shape of this kind of thing in mc was four hundred lines of vocabulary for "one at a time" and Martin threw it out by name (`gate-lock.js`'s header quotes the ruling). Keep this small enough that its whole behaviour fits in the header comment.
comments: **`mc repo nightly start|stop|status`, and it is three files that mirror the watcher's three.** `nightly.js` is the process control (start, stop, state, the paths), `nightly-loop.js` is the tick and the loop around it, `nightly-run.js` is the detached process itself. The split is the watcher's and it is worth keeping: a tick is a plain async function, so a test runs one and reads what it wrote without spawning anything. State and log live in `~/.memoro/mc/nightly/` — `nightly.json` (the pid file) and `nightly.log`, capped at a megabyte and rotated at start.

**Where step 3 hooks on.** `nightlyTick()` returns `{ at, runs, skipped }`, and each entry of `runs` is `{ repo, path, started_at, duration_ms, commit, verdict, stopped_at, reason, red, tests }`. The three outcomes step 3 has to keep apart are already apart in that shape, and the load-bearing part is the type of `red`: `[]` for a run whose suite finished and found nothing, an array of names for one that found failures, and **`null` for a run that produced no suite result at all** — the lock was held, the preparation failed, the declaration stopped it, the round threw. A `null` that gets coerced to an empty set anywhere downstream is the false green this project exists to remove, arriving by a third road. `commit` is `report.base.commit`, the commit of the default branch the round actually checked out.

**There is deliberately no JSON store yet.** The log is text, written by the detached process as its own stdout, and it is for a person reading `nightly.log`. Step 3's bounded history of runs is a different artefact and belongs beside it in `~/.memoro/mc/nightly/`, written with `writeJsonAtomic` like everything else under mc's home. I did not write half of it here, because a half-store with a shape step 3 then has to change is worse than none.

**The cadence: every N since the last completed tick, and the first tick when the scheduler starts.** Not a wall-clock hour, and the code comment says why — a laptop asleep at 03:00 never sees 03:00, and a scheduler that notices the miss on waking fires a catch-up burst at breakfast, which is 300 s of pinned cores at exactly the wrong moment. `--interval <seconds>` is the watcher's own flag with the watcher's own unit, parsed by the same `parseArgs`; only the default differs (86,400,000 ms). The page prints hours for the nightly and seconds for the watcher, because "every 86400s" is not a sentence anybody checks.

**Measured on this machine 2026-09-03, with the real repositories and nobody typing anything.** Tick 1 at 06:16:33 found a real `mc test memoro-cli --full` round holding `gate-running.json` and recorded `memoro  skipped  another gate round is running on this machine (pid 77336, memoro-cli-1d5e7a04, since 2026-09-03T06:16:10.716Z) — one at a time`, in 9 s, without waiting or retrying. Ticks 2 and 3, across a 60 s interval boundary, each measured both repositories whole: memoro 277.1 s and 283.2 s (17,982 tests, 8 red, `main fc19465`), memoro-cli 67.6 s and 67.4 s (2,445 tests, 47 red, `main 0ae0bd4`). Every completed run is one log line carrying its start, its duration, the commit of `main` and its result. About 350 s of machine per tick for the two repositories mc knows.

**The holding round in that check was a `mc test --full` gate round, not a `mc merge` round.** Martin's criterion says "start a merge round"; both take the same lock through the same `takeGateLock` call inside `runGate`, and the tick reads `gate-running.json` and nothing else, so the observation is the same one — but the distinction is his to make and it is written down here rather than smoothed over.

**A killed gate round orphans its suite, and that is why the stop signals the process group.** Measured directly: `mc test memoro-cli --full`, SIGTERMed 8 s into its suite, left two `node --test-concurrency=0` workers at `ppid 1` still running after the round was gone. `repo-gate.js` catches the signal and gives back the lease and the round lock, but nothing kills the suite it spawned, and on POSIX those children are reparented rather than killed. Survivable when a person did the killing; not in a process that stops and starts unattended. The scheduler is spawned detached, so it is its own process-group leader and `stopNightly` signals `-pid`: the round, its `npm run test:full`, and the seven workers under it. Verified with a full memoro suite in flight — nothing left afterwards. **The same hole is still open for `mc test` and `mc merge` killed by hand**, and it is not fixed here: that is `repo-gate.js`'s signal path, not this project's.

**Two things a stop leaves behind that are by design, not defects.** A stop during `prepare` cannot be graceful — `prepare` is a blocking `spawnSync`, so node cannot run the SIGTERM handler until it returns, and after 3 s the group is SIGKILLed. That leaves `gate-running.json` naming a dead pid, which `gate-lock.js` reaps by definition ("taken, and the pid is gone → that round was killed; take it"). And a round that exits by signal never runs its `finally`, so the throwaway gate worktree stays until the next round's `clearWorkspace` — which for memoro is 922 MB. I cleared the one I made by hand.

**One failure I saw once and could not reproduce, so it is reported rather than repaired.** After the first mid-suite kill, the next memoro round stopped at `worktree` with `'…/gate/memoro-a66fc130/candidate' is a missing but already registered worktree`. The round after it was fine — `clearWorkspace` self-heals in one round. The likely cause is the orphaned workers still writing into that tree when `git worktree remove --force` ran, which the group stop above now prevents; I could not make git refuse the removal in a clean reproduction, so I reverted the two-line reorder of `clearWorkspace` I had written for it rather than ship an unproven fix in the shared round. If it recurs after a stop, the suspect line is `repo-gate.js:971` — the prune runs before the directory is removed, and a `git worktree remove` that fails does so by exit code, which `spawnSync` reports and the `catch` around it cannot see.

**A scheduled round is logged as `mode: "nightly"`.** `mc repo rounds` groups by where a round stopped and is unchanged, but two more rounds a day would otherwise arrive in `gate-rounds.jsonl` as checks somebody typed, and "has the gate ever caught anything?" would be answered partly by rounds that were never about a change. `recordRoundStart`/`recordRound` store `mode` and nothing branches on it, so the third value costs nothing.

**`mc repo nightly status` says whether the process is running and where it writes — and nothing about what it found.** That is deliberate: step 3's reading belongs on `mc repo status`'s per-repository section, where a person already looks, not behind a verb somebody has to know to type. The renderer for it is `renderNightlyLines` in `repo-render.js`, beside the watcher's.

**memoro's `main` at `fc19465` is 8 red over 5 files**, and the two runs an interval apart found the identical set — checked name by name in `gate-rounds.jsonl`, which stores `red_names` on every round: `data-bus event names come from a single source file`; three under `S3.1 canonical mutation inventory`; `Signals runtime, routes, commands, and surfaces stay retired`; two under `mc context`; and `append enforces first/next/gap/parent/anchor and exact duplicate semantics`. memoro-cli's `main` at `0ae0bd4` is 47 red of 2,445 tests, also identical across its two runs. That is the first real evidence that step 3's "since when" has something stable to date — and the round log already carries the names, capped, if step 3 wants a second source for them.

steps.title: Red, and since when
steps.done_when: After two runs that both see the same test red, mc names that test with the timestamp of the **first** run that saw it, not the most recent; a test that passes in the latest run is gone from the report entirely; and a run that could not complete is distinguishable from a run in which everything passed.
instruction: The number that would have prevented #10529 is not "31 tests are red". It is "these 31 tests have been red since Tuesday". A single run's red list looks exactly like a flake; the same list twice, dated, does not. So the stored thing is a short history of runs — when, which commit of `main`, and the set of failing test names — and the reported thing is derived from it: for each test red in the latest run, the earliest consecutive run that saw it red.

Keep the history bounded and boring. A fixed number of recent runs, oldest dropped, written atomically, under mc's home beside the other snapshots. Enough to answer "since when" over a week; not a time-series database. Failing test *names* are what is stored — not output, not stack traces, not the log. A name is enough to say a thing is still red, and anything more turns a meter into an archive.

"Consecutive" is the load-bearing word and it is where this will be got wrong. A test red on Monday, green on Tuesday, red on Wednesday has been red since Wednesday, not since Monday. Assert that case directly rather than trusting the reading of it, because the wrong version — earliest occurrence anywhere in the history — looks identical on every history where nothing ever went green, which is every history you will have on the day you write it.

Three run outcomes have to stay distinguishable, and collapsing any two of them is what makes a meter lie: the suite ran and everything passed; the suite ran and named failures; and the run did not produce a suite result at all — the lock was held, the preparation failed, the declaration stopped it, the process died. The third is not zero failures. A day of stopped runs reported as a green streak is the same false green this project's first step exists to remove, arriving by a different road.

Where it shows: the page mc already prints, in the section that says what a repository's state is — not a new verb, and not a section that appears only when something is wrong. A net that is invisible when everything is fine is a net nobody trusts when it finally says something, and "last full run: 4 h ago, all green" is the line that makes the red line credible. Keep it to a line or two per repository; the detail belongs behind whatever `--json` this surface already has.

Two honest sentences memoro will need on day one: its `main` has six tests red as of 2026-09-02 — in `tests/architecture/data-bus.test.js`, `tests/architecture/s3-1-mutation-inventory.test.js` (two), `tests/architecture/signals-runtime-retirement.test.js`, `tests/ui/theme-contract.test.js` and `tests/mc/context.test.js`, and the report has to be readable rather than alarming with that as its normal state. comments: **Where it lives.** `nightly-history.js`: one file per repository under `~/.memoro/mc/nightly/`, named by the same slug rule as the watcher's snapshots (`repoFileSlug`), written with `writeJsonAtomic`, fourteen runs deep with the oldest dropped — two weeks at the default cadence. One stored run is `{at, duration_ms, commit, outcome, stopped_at, reason, tests, red}` and nothing else. The reading (`nightlyReading`) is derived on every read, so the store holds facts and the page holds sentences; nothing is stored that would have to be recomputed if the wording changes.

**Only the tick writes there, and the reason is not tidiness.** `mc test <repo> --full` typed by a person is the same reading, but `--full` chooses no tree — it only turns the selector off (`repo-gate.js:333`) — so it can be asked about a pull request, and then `candidate.red` is about a candidate merge tree that exists nowhere but in the gate worktree. One of those between two nightly entries would make "since when" a sentence about somebody's branch. If a later step ever wants a person's `--full` to count, the thing to key on is `report.pr === null`, not the flag.

**The names are deliberately not capped**, unlike `gate-rounds.jsonl`'s own `red_names` (40, then `… and N more, not named here`). A dropped name returns in the next run looking like a test that had gone green and broken again, and would be dated to today — the exact lie the file exists to prevent. The bound is the number of runs kept. This is also why the two stores disagree in the PR's own test-count paragraph: the round log hid 7 of memoro-cli's 47 names, the history hid none.

**A run that measured nothing is transparent to the streak.** It neither continues one nor breaks one, because it is evidence of nothing: red / stopped / red reads as red since the first red. The alternative — treating a stopped run as a break — would re-date every standing test to the morning after any night the machine was busy, which is the number this project exists to produce being reset by the machine being used. It is still stored, still counted in `runs`, and it is the `last` row on the page above the `measured` one it could not replace. In `--json` the difference is a type: `red: null` for a run that produced no suite result, `red: []` for one that found nothing.

**The page reads it fresh on both paths** — in `gatherRepo` for the computed page and beside `readLease` in `repoView` for the snapshot path — for the lease's reason and one of its own: it costs one file read, and "is main red right now" should not be the one section of the page that is a minute old for no saving at all.

**Verified live on both repositories, 2026-09-03, not only in tests.** memoro: two real ticks at 07:04:26 and 07:08:52, both at `origin/main` `fc19465`, 17,982 tests, the same 8 red both times, dated to 07:04:26 — `data-bus event names come from a single source file` among them, which is the test this plan's check names. memoro-cli: two ticks 66 s apart at `15af210`, 2,455 tests, the same 47 red, `since` 06:54:42 and not 06:55:47.

**And by hand, both ways, on the real stores (backed up and restored).** A third older run pasted at the *end* of memoro's file moved the reported date from 07:04:26 back to 2026-08-30 and the count to 3 — the store sorts by timestamp rather than by file order, precisely because an entry a person adds by hand lands last. Removing `data-bus event names…` from the newest stored run took the page from 8 red to 7, with the name gone rather than lingering with an old date and the other seven keeping their date. On memoro-cli, removing a name from the *middle* run only re-dated that one test to the latest run (`runs: 1, bounded: false`) while the other 46 kept theirs: the consecutive rule, observed rather than reasoned about.

**The skip, observed live.** A real `mc test memoro-cli --full` round held `gate-running.json` (pid 15461) while a tick ran; the tick recorded `busy` in 0.1 s and the page then read `47 red of 2,455` from 3m ago, `last tried just now — busy: another gate round is running…`, and the standing since-date unchanged. Three outcomes, three shapes.

**Not verified live: the green row.** Neither repository mc knows has a green `main`, so `all 2,445 green` — the line the instruction calls the one that makes the red line credible — is asserted in `repo-render.test.js` and has never been printed on this machine. Nothing about it depends on data the tests lack, but nobody has seen it.

**Two things worth knowing for whoever closes this project.** The `full run` section shows for every repository even when the nightly has never run (`never — mc repo nightly start`): deliberate, so the absence of the net is visible on the page rather than being an absence of a page, but it is a line every reader now sees whether or not they use the meter. And the round log and this history now carry the same red names from the same rounds by two paths with two caps; if they ever disagree, the round log is the one the round itself wrote.
